overview:
Bolivia sits in the heart of South America, a landlocked country of high plateaus, snowy peaks and steamy lowlands. It borders Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina, Chile and Peru, and at about 1.1 million km² it is roughly the size of Texas and California combined. Around 12 million people live there.

The country has two capitals. Sucre, the constitutional capital, is a quiet city of white colonial buildings where the supreme court sits. La Paz, at about 3,600 meters above sea level, is where the president and congress work, making it the highest seat of government in the world. Visitors arriving by plane often feel breathless in the thin air.

Bolivia calls itself a Plurinational State because it recognizes 36 Indigenous peoples and languages alongside Spanish, including Quechua, Aymara and Guaraní. Most Bolivians have Indigenous roots, and traditional clothing, music and festivals are part of daily life. The country is a republic with an elected president, and mining, natural gas and farming support the economy.
landAndNature:
Two great chains of the Andes cross western Bolivia, cradling the Altiplano, a windswept plateau nearly 4,000 meters high. Here lies Lake Titicaca, shared with Peru, the highest large lake in the world that boats can navigate, and the Salar de Uyuni, the largest salt flat on Earth, roughly 10,000 km² of blinding white crust that turns into a giant mirror when rain covers it.

East of the mountains the land drops through cloud forests called the Yungas into the hot Amazon basin and the dry Chaco. Madidi National Park, stretching from glaciers to jungle, may hold more species than any other protected area on the planet. Andean condors, vicuñas, pink river dolphins, jaguars and giant anteaters all live in Bolivia, and flamingos feed in red and green mineral lakes high in the southwest.
peopleAndCulture:
Spanish is the common language, but Quechua and Aymara are spoken by millions, especially in the highlands. Aymara women known as cholitas wear bowler hats, layered skirts and bright shawls; some are famous as wrestlers who perform in La Paz. Music played on panpipes, the charango (a small guitar) and drums accompanies dances at every fiesta.

Potatoes were first farmed near Lake Titicaca thousands of years ago, and Bolivians grow hundreds of varieties, along with quinoa, corn and llama meat. Salteñas, juicy baked pastries filled with meat and vegetables, are a mid-morning favorite. The Oruro Carnival, with its devil-masked Diablada dancers, is recognized by UNESCO as a treasure of world culture. Soccer is the top sport, and La Paz's high-altitude stadium leaves visiting teams gasping.
history:
The Tiwanaku civilization built stone temples near Lake Titicaca more than a thousand years ago, and in the 1400s the region became part of the Inca Empire. Spanish conquerors arrived in the 1530s and discovered a mountain of silver at Potosí. For centuries, Indigenous people and enslaved Africans were forced to work its mines, and the silver made Spain rich while millions of workers died.

Independence came in 1825 after long wars, and the new country was named after the liberator Simón Bolívar. Bolivia lost its Pacific coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific (1879–1884) and lost more land to Paraguay in the Chaco War of the 1930s. A 1952 revolution gave land to Indigenous farmers and the vote to everyone. In 2006 Evo Morales became the country's first Indigenous president, and a 2009 constitution created the Plurinational State.
funFacts: The Salar de Uyuni is so flat that satellites use it to calibrate their altitude instruments.
La Paz has the largest urban cable-car network in the world, with gondolas serving as public buses.
Bolivia still has a navy, even though it lost its coastline in 1884; it patrols Lake Titicaca and rivers.
The Yungas Road, dropping 3,500 meters in about 60 kilometers, was once nicknamed the world's most dangerous road.
Bolivia's Wiphala, a rainbow checkerboard flag of the Andean peoples, is an official national flag alongside the red, yellow and green one.
Some Andean women wrestlers, the Fighting Cholitas, compete in full traditional skirts and bowler hats.
